canberra.title: Teen fined $5000 for plastering white supremacy stickers at ANU
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains phrases some may find offensive. A teenager has been fined thousands of dollars for plastering pro...
canberra.content:
30 October 2026

Zachery James Hook (main photo) admitted to placing white supremacy stickers (inserts) around the ANU. The two stickers have been partially blurred to hide some offensive content. Photos: Albert McKnight/Tendered to the court.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains phrases some may find offensive.

A teenager has been fined thousands of dollars for plastering pro-white supremacy stickers around the Australian National University (ANU).

But while 19-year-old Zachery James Hook had also been scheduled to be sentenced for making Nazi salutes at members of the public, the ACT Magistrates Court instead decided to send him to the Territory’s higher court to deal with this second matter.

Hook was 18 when he went to the ANU campus twice in August and September 2025, court documents say.

He pasted stickers – containing phrases like ‘National Socialist Network’, ‘Australia for the white man’, and, ‘White revolution is the only solution’ – onto signs for the Tjabal Indigenous Higher Education Centre and in the Black, Indigenous and People of Colour building.

He pleaded guilty to a charge of offensive behaviour over these actions. But he also pleaded guilty to a charge of making a Nazi salute in public after he made Nazi salutes at the O’Connor shops in October 2025 and the Chisholm shops that December.

On Friday (30 October), Magistrate James Lawton told the court that Hook had behaved in a “targetted manner” when placing the stickers at the ANU.

“He’s actions were clearly offensive,” he said.

“The prevalence of social media no doubt had an impact on Mr Hook and the formation of the views that allowed him to behave in this way.”

But he also noted that it was somewhat troubling that Hook had not necessarily changed his views before his sentencing.

Tjabal Centre director Professor Anne Martin told the court that the stickers affected her sense of safety, as she didn’t know whether they were isolated incidents or would lead to more activity.

But the court heard she also expressed forgiveness for Hook’s actions.

“My hope is that you take time to seriously consider the impact that your actions have had on other people and the direction you want your life to take,” she told him.

“Hatred and intimidation do not need to determine the person you will become.”

Hook was convicted and fined $5000 for his offensive behaviour charge.

The charge of making a Nazi salute has a maximum sentence of five years’ jail if it is dealt with in the Supreme Court, but both prosecutors and defence lawyers had consented to Hook being sentenced on this charge in the Magistrates Court.

Magistrate Lawton said “somewhat unusual circumstances” meant he could impose only a 12-month sentence for Hook because of how the legislation was written.

He said Hook had made such salutes to members of the public on two days, and he did not think the offending fell at the lower end of the seriousness scale.

The magistrate said he did not think his court was empowered to impose an appropriate penalty and referred the charge to the Supreme Court for sentencing.

The matter will first appear in the higher court on 18 November to begin organising a sentencing date, and Hook’s bail was continued.

He is the second person in the ACT to plead guilty to the charge of making a Nazi salute in public.

canberra.title: From six-packs to wrinkle-free skin: Peptide craze strains Canberra’s free needle supply
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s free needle and syringe program is being stretched by an unexpected new clientele: people injecting peptides to build bi...
canberra.content:
Canberra’s free needle and syringe program is facing growing demand from people injecting peptides for fitness, weight loss and cosmetic purposes. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra’s free needle and syringe program is being stretched by an unexpected new clientele: people injecting peptides to build bigger muscles, lose weight, recover faster and look younger.

Demand has surged so sharply over the past year that Directions Health Services has begun rationing some injecting equipment to ensure people who rely on the service to prevent blood-borne infections are not left without supplies.

The growing pressure sparked a debate in the ACT Legislative Assembly, where the Opposition questioned whether taxpayer-funded syringes were being diverted to people following online beauty and fitness trends.

During Question Time on 29 October, Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton asked Health Minister Marisa Paterson when the government became aware of the problem and what additional resources had been provided to Directions, which coordinates the ACT’s Needle and Syringe Program.

Dr Paterson acknowledged the surge could affect the organisation’s ability to serve its traditional clients, including people injecting psychoactive drugs.

“We haven’t had any specific requests for additional resources at this point, but we are absolutely aware of this as an increasing issue and will continue to work closely with Directions to monitor it,” she said.

Canberra Liberals MLA Deborah Morris went further, asking how much government funding had effectively been wasted providing free syringes to peptide users.

“Well, I don’t think it’s been wasted. Obviously if people are injecting substances in the community, we want them to do that safely,” Dr Paterson responded.

But the exchange highlighted a difficult question for Canberra’s harm-reduction services: how do they accommodate a rapidly expanding group of people injecting substances for cosmetic and performance purposes without compromising care for those already at risk?

Speaking to Region, Directions Health Services chief operating officer Stephanie Stephens acknowledged that the organisation was witnessing a significant shift in demand.

“We are seeing a new group of people accessing needle and syringe programs specifically to obtain equipment to inject peptides,” she said.

New clients are seeking larger quantities of injecting equipment for peptide use, forcing Directions to limit supplies per visit.

“We have had to introduce limits on the amount of some equipment provided at one time so that we can maintain supply for the broader community, particularly people injecting drug intravenously,” Ms Stephens said.

The program was established to reduce infections such as HIV and hepatitis C by providing sterile injecting equipment and advice. Its funding and supply arrangements were not designed around the rapid growth of a new group of users seeking products promoted for appearance, fitness and wellbeing.

But Directions is not arguing that peptide users should be turned away.

“We absolutely want people who inject peptides to use sterile equipment and have access to good harm-reduction advice,” Ms Stephens said.

“The problem is that this is a rapidly growing new cohort, often requesting much larger quantities of equipment, and NSP funding and supply were never designed around this level of demand,” she added.

There is another concern beyond the pressure on supplies: many people arriving for needles may have little understanding of the substances they are injecting.

Peptides are a broad category of compounds, some of which are used in approved medicines. But the emerging trend involves a wide range of products marketed online for muscle growth, fat loss, injury recovery, tanning, anti-ageing and sleep, including substances that have not been approved for those purposes.

Directions staff have encountered new clients with limited knowledge of safer injecting practices, while relatively few report having discussed their peptide use with a health professional.

“Our concerns include injection-related complications, variable product quality, contamination, dosing uncertainty and unknown longer-term effects,” Ms Stephens said.

Social media is helping drive that demand.

According to Directions, people are learning about peptides through influencers, online forums, coaches and peers, while some are also purchasing the substances online.

Ms Stephens said promoting these products could create a misleading impression that they were relatively low-risk.

That concern also surfaced during Question Time, when Ms Morris asked what advice the minister had for influencers encouraging people to obtain free syringes from Directions.

Dr Paterson urged those promoting, selling or buying unregulated peptides to stop, warning that products bought online may not contain what their labels claim.

She also raised concerns about a peptide marketed for rapid tanning and its reported association with increased skin cancer risk.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) has repeatedly warned about unapproved and counterfeit peptide products sold online.

In August, the regulator and NSW Police allegedly seized more than $120,000 worth of illicit peptide and anabolic steroid products in NSW from a social media influencer accused of advertising and selling unapproved substances.

Yet the ACT Government cannot currently say how many people may have suffered complications serious enough to require emergency treatment.

In response to Region, the Health and Community Services Directorate confirmed it does not collect reportable data that specifically identifies presentations to Canberra’s two emergency departments linked to unregulated peptide use.

The directorate said it was monitoring reports of harm interstate and continued to work with Directions and other jurisdictions on the challenges facing needle and syringe programs.

For Ms Stephens, the solution is not to make sterile needles harder to obtain. That could increase the risk of people reusing or sharing injecting equipment.

Instead, she wants services to be adequately resourced to meet changing demand, along with better access to reliable information about the products and the risks of injecting them.

canberra.title: Police say stolen dog still missing when alleged robber refused bail
canberra.snippet: Police are continuing their search to find a dog that was allegedly stolen when his owner was punched and kicked in the head during a day...
canberra.content:
30 October 2026

Police are still trying to find this dog, which was stolen in an alleged robbery in Belconnen on 30 August 2026. Photos: Michelle Kroll/ACT Policing.

Police are continuing their search to find a dog that was allegedly stolen when his owner was punched and kicked in the head during a daylight robbery.

ACT Policing have previously alleged the dog’s owner was walking in Belconnen around 12:30 pm on 30 August 2026 when he was assaulted and had his dog stolen.

The ACT Magistrates Court has heard it was alleged 26-year-old Ahmad Bashar Al Araja had gotten out of a white Land Rover with another man and kicked the owner in the head region.

Mr Al Araja also allegedly grabbed the owner by the shirt and punched him in the face.

He was arrested the following day, entered a not guilty plea to the robbery charge, and remained in custody before applying for bail again on Friday (30 October).

Because of unrelated charges, he had to show special or exceptional circumstances to favour bail.

His lawyer, Richard Brandon-Baker, said his client had been in a car accident a few days before his arrest which left him with a collarbone injury. His client claimed his collarbone was still dislocated and he hadn’t been getting Endone for pain relief while in custody.

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen questioned the severity of this injury, seeing as Mr Al Araja was allegedly to have repeatedly assaulted the dog’s owner.

“If that allegation is accepted, he’s still pretty mobile,” he said.

Mr Brandon-Baker said Mr Al Araja and his father ran a mechanic business in Canberra. It had been experiencing commercial difficulties – particularly after his client went into custody.

“He’s central to the operation of that business,” the lawyer said.

He said Mr Al Araja was born in Iraq in 2000 before his family fled to Syria as refugees.

“He’s really moved from one war zone into another and witnessed horrendous things that caused significant trauma that he is still dealing with to this day,” Mr Brandon-Baker said.

He said his client had mental health struggles and was left homeless for a time after his house in Turner was “set alight” last year.

He also said the allegations were disputed and he expected the matter would go to a hearing next year.

Prosecutor Susie Kim said there was no evidence about when the car accident actually occurred and she noted Mr Al Araja had been receiving treatment in custody, as he had been going to a physiotherapist.

Special Magistrate Cowen said the alleged robbery involved significant violence and there were no special or exceptional circumstances to justify Mr Al Araja receiving bail.

He was remanded in custody, and the matter was adjourned to 10 November.

A 22-year-old man has also been charged with being knowingly concerned in a robbery over the allegations, and he, too, has been remanded in custody.

Meanwhile, an ACT Policing spokesperson said the dog was still missing, despite their extensive investigations. These investigations were continuing.

The dog is a Staffordshire bull terrier with a short dark brindle coat, black muzzle, a white chest and white speckled front legs.

If you can assist police, provide your contact details to Crime Stoppers via the Crime Stoppers ACT website. Quote 8485238.

canberra.title: No AI, no algorithms: Minister grilled over removal of 1000 children from specialist waitlist
canberra.snippet: Artificial intelligence was not used to remove more than 1000 children from Canberra’s paediatric allergy clinic waiting list, the ...
canberra.content:
The removal of more than 1000 children from Canberra’s paediatric allergy clinic waitlist has sparked questions in the ACT Assembly. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Artificial intelligence was not used to remove more than 1000 children from Canberra’s paediatric allergy clinic waiting list, the ACT Government said, as the controversial decision dominated Question Time in the Legislative Assembly this week.

The removal of children, including some suffering from anaphylaxis, has triggered questions about how patients were assessed, why families were not given individual explanations and whether they have any realistic pathway back to specialist care.

Health Minister Marisa Paterson faced repeated questions from Liberals, Greens and independent MLAs over the process, with MLA Thomas Emerson comparing the way families were notified to the controversial Robodebt scheme.

Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti asked whether automated decision-making tools, algorithms, scoring systems or other decision-support systems had been used to determine which children remained eligible for specialist appointments.

“No, I can absolutely confirm that was not the case,” Ms Paterson said.

She told the Assembly that each case had been reviewed by a highly specialised medical practitioner, rather than an automated system.

The explanation followed revelations that children experiencing anaphylaxis were among those removed from the waiting list, despite the condition being a key criterion for accessing specialist allergy services.

The issue has raised concerns about how revised clinical guidelines were applied and whether families whose children have serious allergies will be able to secure specialist appointments.

Mr Emerson drew a comparison with Robodebt, not over how the decisions were made but how they were communicated.

“You owe the government a debt, unless you can prove you don’t. You’re off the waitlist, unless you can prove you shouldn’t be,” he said.

The questions continued when Greens leader Jo Clay pressed the minister on what safeguards were available to families removed from specialist waiting lists.

She asked whether parents were told the reasons for the decisions and informed of their rights to seek a review or reconsideration.

Ms Paterson said letters sent to affected families included Canberra Health Services (CHS) contact details and information about requesting a review.

She also confirmed that referring GPs had received correspondence explaining the revised clinical criteria.

Families who believed their children still required specialist care were advised to return to their GP to discuss whether another referral was necessary.

However, Ms Clay challenged whether the letters actually explained why individual children had been removed.

The minister said the correspondence stated that a clinical review had been undertaken and that the guidelines governing access to the service had changed.

The controversy has also drawn criticism from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP), which warned that the changes risked shifting responsibility back to GPs without ensuring appropriate alternatives were available.

RACGP NSW and ACT chair Dr Rebekah Hoffman said families deserved transparency and a clear pathway to care.

“Families waiting for specialist care are already under enormous stress. Receiving a letter telling them their child has been removed from a waitlist, without adequate explanation or consultation with the doctors who will be left managing their care, is deeply concerning,” she said.

“Patients should not be disappearing from waitlists simply because the system cannot meet demand. We need solutions that improve access to care, not administrative exercises that make waiting lists look shorter on paper.”

Dr Hoffman urged the government to fund five GPs with Special Interests within the public health system.

These are experienced GPs with additional training in particular clinical areas who could assess and treat patients who do not require a traditional hospital specialist appointment.

The dispute comes amid a broader CHS review of outpatient services, following recommendations from the independent review of the ACT health system led by Michael Walsh.

CHS delivers approximately 250,000 outpatient appointments annually, while around 65,000 people are currently waiting for specialist care.

The review is examining referral pathways and eligibility criteria to prioritise patients with the greatest clinical need.

CHS says some patients may be contacted to confirm whether appointments are still required or whether alternative treatment pathways would be more appropriate. Affected patients and referring clinicians will be notified as changes are introduced progressively.

canberra.title: Driver dies after double-truck crash north of Canberra
canberra.snippet: A driver died after two trucks crashed north of Canberra early on Friday morning (30 October). Police officers were called to the Hume Hi...
canberra.content:
30 October 2026

30 October 2026

Join the conversation

1

The truck crash occurred outside Gunning, NSW on 30 October 2026. Photo: Live Traffic NSW.

A driver died after two trucks crashed north of Canberra early on Friday morning (30 October).

Police officers were called to the Hume Highway, just east of the NSW town of Gunning, around 6 am, a NSW Police spokesperson said.

One B-double truck had crashed into the rear of a second B-double truck. Sadly, the driver of the second truck died at the scene.

“The other driver was uninjured and has been taken to hospital for mandatory testing,” the spokesperson said.

“Police have established a crime scene and an investigation into the cause of the crash has commenced.”

The highway remains open, but significant traffic delays are expected and motorists are urged to avoid the area.

australia.title: Erin Patterson to die in prison after losing appeal against mushroom murder convictions
australia.snippet: Victorian court of appeal rules Patterson should be jailed for life with no parole over deadly beef wellington lunch that killed three pe...
australia.content:
Erin Patterson has lost her bid to overturn her convictions and been resentenced to life behind bars with no chance of release, as Victoria’s highest court handed down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.

The court of appeal ruled on the two appeals on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.

Patterson, 52, did not attend the 15-minute court hearing in person, and showed no emotion on the video feed as McLeish outlined why her appeal had failed, and how the director of public prosecutions had succeeded in seeking a longer sentence.

Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.

She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.

McLeish said the court had granted leave to appeal on the first two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, but dismissed the appeal, and dismissed the five other grounds raised by her lawyers.

He said the court granted the DPP appeal against the sentence, however, as it was clear the original sentence did not properly reflect the seriousness of her offending.

McLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”.

The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said.

When the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, and walked off-screen.

In the courtroom, family members hugged and were emotional, and detectives involved in the case looked elated. Nobody commented outside court.

Patterson now must apply to the high court for leave to appeal, should she wish to continue fighting her conviction or new sentence.

She is one of only a handful of Victorian offenders sentenced to life without parole, and one of the only women in Australian history to be given the sentence.

Written reasons for the decision were provided to media later on Friday.

In them, the court said while the first ground of the DPP’s appeal – that trial judge erred in finding that there was a substantial chance Patterson would be in solitary confinement for much of her sentence – had failed, it was clear the second ground, that the sentence was manifestly inadequate, should succeed.

The court found they were “heinous crimes” and “we are driven to conclude that a non-parole period of 33 years fails to reflect the calculated criminality of the applicant in committing three murders and attempting a fourth”.

“The offending was carefully planned and deliberate. It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of the applicant’s extended family,” the court found.

“The taking of three lives (and the attempt on another) in these circumstances called in our view for much stronger denunciation.”

In relation to Patterson’s appeal, the court described many of the grounds as having no substance, being without merit, or even fanciful.

In relation to the ground that the sequestering of the jury in the same hotel as the police informant and members of the prosecution amounted to a substantial miscarriage of justice, the court found that it “was plainly unfortunate that [the] situation arose”. It said it was “highly undesirable” and “the judge would not have countenanced this arrangement if approval for it had been sought in advance”.

But the justices said there was no evidence any wrongdoing had occurred.

“The accommodation arrangements offered fertile grounds for speculation but no objective basis for the fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function of rendering a verdict according to law. “

In relation to ground two – that undue weight was placed on evidence given by a telecommunications expert that raised the possibility she visited two sites where death cap mushrooms had been reported – the court found the probative value of the evidence was not outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice to Patterson.

In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.

Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.

Richard Edney, for Patterson, had said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial.

“What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August.

During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.

australia.title: Former Sydney childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith hit with 202 more abuse charges
australia.snippet: NSW police say charges include child rape and relate to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five at a Sydney childcare centre Get our...
australia.content:
One of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles is facing hundreds more child abuse charges, including for the alleged rape of children as young as one.

Days after being extradited from Queensland to New South Wales, Ashley Paul Griffith was hit with 202 charges dating from between 2014 and 2017, with police labelling the allegations “deeply disturbing”.

The Queensland man was working at a childcare centre in Sydney’s inner west at the time of the alleged offending, which included dozens of alleged rapes against children between one and five.

Griffith, 48, was jailed for life in Queensland in November 2024 after he pleaded guilty to more than 300 child sexual offences against nearly 70 victims.

The fresh charges from NSW include 68 counts of rape of a child aged less than 10 and 42 counts of aggravated rape of a child aged less than 10 who was under his authority.

Other charges include 69 counts of aggravated indecent assault and 23 charges of producing child abuse material.

Police said the charges pertained to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five.

He was charged while being held in Silverwater Correctional Complex in Sydney.

NSW Det Supt Linda Howlett said charging Griffith with further alleged offending could help potential victims.

“There’s no other word for it, it’s actually horrific,” she said in relation to the allegations.

The child abuse squad commander thanked witnesses, alleged victims and detectives for their work in preparing the challenging but “airtight” case.

Police are extending every assistance to those involved, Howlett said.

Griffith did not apply for bail in a brief court appearance on Friday.

The NSW police assistant commissioner Brett Greentree said the lengthy investigation included collaboration with police across the nation.

“The allegations before the court are deeply disturbing and involve some of the most vulnerable members of our community,” he said.

“Every child deserves to be safe and protected from harm. NSW Police is committed to ensuring those who exploit positions of trust to offend against children are identified, investigated and brought before the courts.”

Griffith arrived in NSW on Wednesday.

In Queensland, he admitted to assaulting and filming young girls over the course of years while working at childcare centres.

His transfer was approved by a Brisbane magistrate earlier in the month, where the alleged victims’ supporters yelled insults at the rapist as he stood in the dock for the decision.

In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

australia.title: Erin Patterson began the day with hope. Now Australia’s mushroom murderer knows she’s likely to die in jail
australia.snippet: Patterson watched on, clad in prison-issued blue, as Victoria’s highest court rejected her appeal against her murder convictions Erin Pat...
australia.content:
Erin Patterson raised her chin and stared out on the brilliant blue promise of a mid-spring morning.

To the east, Victoria’s grandest court room was filled with people she had brought together, yet she was there only on a screen.

Patterson watched on, clad in prison-issued blue, from the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre.

Soon, three justices of the court of appeal would enter the Banco court, and Patterson would learn whether she would walk under that sky again as a free woman.

Patterson, 52, was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.

She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.

Anyone who sat through her appeal hearings in August considered her prospects to be slim.

She argued on seven grounds that her conviction should be set aside, but there was little thrust to her arguments, little sense that the justices were for turning.

Indeed, they appeared more receptive to an appeal by the director of public prosecutions that Patterson’s non-parole period of 33 years was manifestly inadequate.

Even if the status quo remained, with Patterson’s appeal against her conviction failing and the DPP’s bid for her sentence to be increased also falling short, there was little to look forward to – she would be in her early 80s before she could apply for parole.

It took only 15 minutes for Justice Stephen McLeish to stifle even that breath of hope.

McLeish said the court dismissed all but two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, granted leave to appeal on the final two but dismissed those too, and agreed with the DPP that Patterson should be resentenced.

It was not just that her non-parole period was too short, McLeish said: it was that she should not have any prospect of ever being released.

McLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”.

The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” – including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms.

In the plain language of the courts, McLeish said that under the sentencing act he and his fellow justices had found that the nature of Patterson’s crimes meant that fixing any non-parole period was inappropriate.

“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said.

There was a sense in the court at this point of time standing still, of the import of the decision lingering, its weight being felt on the shoulders and in the balls of the feet.

But it was hard too not to think back to the day in Ian Wilkinson’s church when Patterson invited her in-laws to lunch, to them sitting at her table less than a fortnight later, and saying grace.

To the individual beef wellingtons in front of them, her own plate a different colour to theirs. To her sitting with them, watching them eat what she hoped would be their last meals.

And then the frantic search for answers when they fell unwell, and Patterson appearing dumbfounded, denying she had foraged, suggesting Asian grocers in far-flung suburbs as the source of the mushrooms, her lies mounting as her victims slipped ever closer to death.

As she stared blankly at the camera in front of her, there was no sense of how Patterson felt. She maintains the beef wellingtons were accidentally laced with death cap mushrooms, that she too fell sick after eating them, that her lies after the lunch were caused by panic.

Patterson may see the inside of a court room again – she has 28 days to seek leave to appeal to the high court.

Should fresh and compelling evidence emerge – a high bar rarely cleared – she could also seek a fresh court of appeal hearing.

Even should she do so, there remains little prospect that a question at the heart of the case will ever be resolved.

It is a question that has not been answered by the millions of words spoken and written and broadcast about murders covered perhaps more ghoulishly than any other in Australian history.

That question is why Erin Patterson murdered people who loved her and showed her kindness, who loved her children, who she invited into her home and looked in the eye as they ate the meal that killed them.

When McLeish finished speaking and the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, turned her back on the window and that brilliant blue, and walked off-screen.

australia.title: Feral deer will become Australia’s next feral pig problem without prompt action, report warns
australia.snippet: The invasive species has increased in spread and numbers and is costing farmers millions of dollars Get our breaking news email , free ap...
australia.content:
An unpublished government report on feral deer shows Australia is failing in its efforts to stop the spread of what one advocate warns could become “Australia’s next feral pig”.

The five years from 2020-2025 over which the national feral deer action plan was assessed covers a period in which the famously elusive species has increasingly encroached upon major cities, leading to more frequent encounters – including a memorable occasion in which two men in various degrees of undress were fined after becoming lost in the bush when they were spooked by deer while nude sunbathing.

The report says deer, one of the country’s “most rapidly increasing invasive pests”, have both increased in numbers and spread in territory, costing more than $91m in production loss and management time every year.

Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie, president of the Australian Mammal Society, said he was “not at all” surprised by this year’s national vertebrate pest management report card.

“This report shows that governments are failing miserably to invest enough to control deer populations and the severe impacts that they can have on agriculture, native wildlife and the environment, road safety and culturally significant sites,” Ritchie said.

“This is what sustained failure to act sufficiently results in.”

Six species of feral deer are established in Australia – chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa and sambar – with well-established populations across south-eastern Australia, where densities are highest. There are smaller, more localised populations in South and Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

The report card, produced by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, shows every state and territory is failing or floundering in their efforts to control feral deer – with one notable exception. South Australia, which launched an ambitious statewide eradication plan in 2022, received a green in all four categories assessed under the traffic light system of marking. The report showed – with high confidence – that the state had decreased the abundance, distribution and environmental and agricultural impacts of deer.

New South Wales and Tasmania were given reds in all four categories, while Queensland and the ACT both received three reds and a yellow. No jurisdiction but SA received a single green pass mark.

Invasive Species Council advocacy manager Reece Pianta said the report confirmed what land managers had been seeing on the ground for some years. In May 2025, the council released footage and images that it said showed the Gold Coast “under feral deer siege”.

Pianta said the report, leaked to his organisation, points to “a long-term systemic underfunding of deer control”. He said deer did not have the recognition of other more notorious invasives, but controlling them was every bit as necessary.

“Deer are the next feral pig,” he said. “The difference with deer is that an intervention now could make a significant difference to the population numbers and contain, or even reverse, that spread.”

While Pianta said deer “probably can’t be eradicated” from the entire continent, he said South Australia’s “A+” report score showed it was possible to do so in some states and territories, while others would require a long-term effort to contain the spread of deer and mitigate their impacts.

Adelaide University Environment Institute director Prof Andrew Lowe said the report was a “good news story” for his state that rang true with what he was seeing on the ground.

Lowe, who is also member of the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, which is involved in managing deer, said SA grappled with its “massive problem with deer” in earnest from 2022, after an agricultural impact estimate showed the $36m worth of damage done every year by deer there was set to increase to $241m by 2031.

But although deer had “massively declined” in the few years since a $4m eradication program began, Lowe said deer were seeking refuge on the fringes of urban areas, where culling was more expensive. He said functional eradication of deer from SA would take about another $10m over 10 years.

The cost of inaction, though, was of a different magnitude.

“If we don’t do that, then the population will go up again and we’re going to be in the same situation,” Lowe said. “So $10m versus $240m – do the math.”

australia.title: What have they come as? Halloween costume inspiration from the kids of 1887
australia.snippet: Are you rummaging about for bits of wire and pumpkin-coloured crêpe paper and wondering if a scorch-marked tea-towel will work as a devil...
australia.content:
Actually, don’t – their costumes were made by professional costumiers, befitting the hundreds of posh kids who sashayed into the lord mayoress’s fancy-dress ball for children at Adelaide town hall nearly 140 years ago. But their rare and incredibly detailed photos could provide some Halloween inspiration.

My happy place is a hushed archive reading room looking at objects. I was looking for copyright-free researching images for my latest book, Spooky Ladies, and silently squeed as these costume photos were delivered in a very long, narrow, custom-made heritage-green box by the good folk at the State Library of South Australia, packed tightly with more than 300 stiff “cabinet cards”, showing kids dressed as fairies, devils, astrologers, witches, and fortune tellers.

On that rainy spring night in 1887, just under 400 kids, of the 700 or so invited, tromped into the town hall hung about with favourite colonial decorations: ferns, British flags, and lots of mirrors reflecting the flowers and chandeliers. There were cloakrooms, a dancefloor and supper room. Hundreds of parents paid for tickets to watch from the upper reaches of the halls.

Two standouts were wee Isabel Stuckey, 7, as a “white witch”, and tween-aged Ethel Hamilton, 12, dressed as one of Satan’s helpers.

Isabel and Ethel were just two of the girls there from the most privileged white families of colonial South Australia; sons and daughters of publicans, politicians, public servants, and pastoralists. An annual event for a while there in the Victorian era, the 1887 ball was hosted by the mayor’s second wife, Elizabeth (eventually Lady) Smith. She’s the only adult whose photo is saved in the collection; frocked up as Elizabeth I.

Other ball attenders were wearing cozzies showing their era’s own nostalgia, or their own times and class. Lots of milkmaids, English and French royals, cricketers, sailors, Kate Greenaway illustrations, popular songs, jesters and fishwives.

Most kids adopted the solemn, standard photo-face of the late 19th century, but some look almost gleeful. Geraldine Hargrave sported a wry smile posing as a masherette – the girl version of a masher, a kiss-chasing, dandy archetype chap of the day that girls tried to avoid. Other girls dressed as their aspiration: female scholars in gowns and mortarboards, a novelty in the days when very few women were allowed into universities.

One astronomically clever boy, Leslie Gardner, 10, fronted up as an eclipse with one side of his face black, the other white.

A book by Adern Holt published that year carried instructions for a hornet costume and others including a wastepaper basket, a female demon, and the Suez canal. (For a vampire, wear bat-wing sleeves and “put bat in hair”.)

Ten-year-old Edith Brock was snapped sporting an insouciant and mermaidy gaze. She was emblematic of the costumed girls, growing up part of the debutante-set, set to be a “spinster” or marry into another of various local grandee families of Bonythons, Downers and Ayerses.

Witness Edith’s “wealth of golden hair” as described in the newspapers. At one time engaged to an English soldier, she stayed a rich miss to the end of her days in 1927. Many little girls from these photos from 1887 didn’t marry until they were older, or at all, reflecting probably the death toll of the first world war, and a financial independence due to family wealth.

Another typical attender was Fred Tennant, a 13-year-old dressed as Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Garibaldi. He grew up to be a lawyer and horse-breeder. His grandfather John Tennant came from England a lowly Scottish shepherd, and with his eldest son Andrew became rich on land “cleared” of Aboriginal people by threats and killings, and married off his kids to “respectable” society figures. Fred was disowned for marrying a non-connected woman, Kathleen.

By the early 1900s, (always Miss) Birdie Dean was a regular in the social pages: she holidayed in London, frocked up in cream satin or black marocain at afternoon teas, stayed with friends in the wine district, and baked a cake to help raise money for soldiers.

May the spirit of the 1887 seamstresses be with you this weekend while you’re stapling together some last-minute Halloween get-ups. If you can’t manage a taxidermied bat in your up-do, take heart. It’s probably the only night of the year when a dad can lead the kids through the neighbourhood wearing a tea-towel as a cape, and his Speedos over his trousers, demanding lollies with menace.

  • Spooky Ladies: Rebels, witches, mediums & magic by Kaz Cooke is published by Simon & Schuster ($37.99)

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.
